en: Oṃ. The gods, indeed, went to the heavenly world and asked Rudra: "Who are you? He replied: "I alone existed in the beginning; I shall endure and I shall be in the future; there is nothing whatsoever other than me.
He entered from the interior into the interior; he entered the space between the quarters. I am that—both eternal and non-eternal, manifest and unmanifest.

I am Brahmā; I am the one facing east, the one facing west, the one facing south, and the one facing north; I am below and above, and I am the cardinal directions and the intermediate directions; I am male, I am neuter, and I am females; I am Sāvitrī, I am Gāyatrī, and I am Triṣṭubh, Jagatī, and Anuṣṭubh;
I am the meter; I am truth; I am the Gārhapatya fire, the Dakṣiṇāgni, and the Āhavanīya fire; I am the bull, and I am the cow.
I am the Ṛgveda, I am the Yajurveda, I am the Sāmaveda, I am the Atharvāṅgirases; I am the eldest, I am the best, I am the most excellent;
I am the waters, I am the fire, I am the secret, I am the forest; I am the imperishable, I am the perishable, I am Puṣkara, I am the purifier;
I am the fierce and I am the offering; I am the light in the east—indeed, I alone am all, and one should know me alone.
He who knows all of that with its secret essence (samaya) knows me; he knows all the gods and all the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs (sāṅga).

With Brahman I satisfy the Brāhmaṇas, with cows the cows, with Brāhmaṇahood the Brāhmaṇas, with oblation the oblation, with life-span life, with truth truth, and with dharma dharma—I satisfy them all by my own splendor.

Then indeed those gods questioned Rudra; those gods beheld Rudra; those gods meditated upon Rudra; those gods praised Rudra with their arms raised. Om! He who is Rudra is the Blessed Lord, and he who is Brahmā—to him indeed be salutation after salutation.
He who is Rudra is the Blessed Lord, and he who is Viṣṇu—to him indeed be salutation after salutation.
He who is Rudra is the Blessed One; he who is Skanda—to him indeed be salutation after salutation. He who is Rudra is the Blessed One; he who is Indra—to him indeed be salutation after salutation.
He who is Rudra is the Blessed One; he who is Agni—to him indeed be salutation after salutation.
He who is Rudra is indeed the Blessed One; and he who is Vāyu—to him, indeed, be salutation after salutation.

(SirUp_7) He who is Rudra is indeed the Blessed One; and he who is Sūrya—to him, indeed, be salutation after salutation. (SirUp_8) He who is Rudra is indeed the Blessed One; and he who is Soma—to him, indeed, be salutation after salutation. (SirUp_9)
He who is Rudra is the Blessed One; and those who are the eight *grahas*—to him indeed be salutation after salutation!

(SirUp 10) He who is Rudra is the Blessed One; and those who are the eight *pratigrahas*—to him indeed be salutation after salutation! (SirUp 11) He who is Rudra is the Blessed One; and that which is the earth (*bhūḥ*)—to him indeed be salutation after salutation! (SirUp 12)
He who is Rudra is the Blessed One; and that which is Bhuvas—to him indeed be salutation after salutation.
He who is Rudra is the Blessed One; and that which is Svaḥ—to him indeed be salutation after salutation.
He who is Rudra is the Blessed One; and that which is Mahas—to him indeed be salutation after salutation.
He who is Rudra is the Blessed One; and that which is the earth—to him indeed be salutation after salutation.
He who is Rudra is the Blessed One; and that which is the intermediate space—to him indeed be salutation after salutation.
He who is Rudra is the Blessed One; and that which is the sky—to him indeed be salutation after salutation.
He who is Rudra is the Blessed One; and whatever is water—to him indeed be salutation after salutation.
He who is Rudra is the Blessed One; and whatever is fire—to him indeed be salutation after salutation.
He who is Rudra is the Blessed One; and whatever is time—to him indeed be salutation after salutation.

He who is Rudra is the Blessed One, and he who is Yama—to him indeed be salutation after salutation. He who is Rudra is the Blessed One, and he who is Death—to him indeed be salutation after salutation.
He who is Rudra is the Blessed One, and that which is immortality—to him indeed be salutation after salutation.
He who is Rudra is the Blessed One; and that which is space—to him indeed be salutation after salutation.

(SirUp_24) He who is Rudra is the Blessed One; and that which is the universe—to him indeed be salutation after salutation. (SirUp_25) He who is Rudra is the Blessed One; and that which is gross—to him indeed be salutation after salutation. (SirUp_26)

He who is Rudra is the Blessed One; and that which is subtle—to him indeed be salutation after salutation. He who is Rudra is the Blessed One; and that which is white—to him indeed be salutation after salutation. He who is Rudra is the Blessed One; and that which is black—to him indeed be salutation after salutation.

He who is Rudra is the Blessed One, and whatever is the All—to him indeed be salutation after salutation. He who is Rudra is the Blessed One, and whatever is Truth—to him indeed be salutation after salutation.
He who is Rudra is the Blessed One, and whatever is Everything—to him indeed be salutation after salutation.

Bhūḥ is your beginning, bhuvaḥ is your middle, and svaḥ is your head; you are the one whose form is the universe, you are the Brahman alone. You are twofold and threefold growth; you are peace, you are nourishment; you are the offered oblation and the unoffered, the given and the not given;
you are all and not-all, the universal and the non-universal, the created and the uncreated, the supreme, the inferior, and the ultimate refuge.

Having drunk the Soma of the waters, we have become immortal; light has come to us, and we have found the gods. What now can hostility do to us? And what, O Immortal One, can the malice of a mortal do? Before Soma and Sūrya stands the subtle Puruṣa.
This syllable is indeed for the welfare of the entire world; it is that which belongs to Prajāpati, which is gentle, subtle, and the Puruṣa to be grasped.
It swallows the gentle state with a gentle state, the subtle with a subtle, and the airy with an airy—homage, again and again, to that Great Swallower!
All deities reside in the heart; the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are established in the heart.
You are eternally in the heart; that which is beyond the three measures (*mātrās*) is He.
To His north is the head, and to His south are the feet. That which is in the north is the syllable *oṃ*; that which is the syllable *oṃ* is the *praṇava*.

That which is the *praṇava* is all-pervading; that which is all-pervading is infinite; that which is infinite is the *tāra*; that which is the *tāra* is white; that which is white is subtle; that which is subtle is the lightning-like (*vaidyuta*); that which is the lightning-like is the supreme Brahman; that which is the supreme Brahman is the One; that which is the One is Rudra; that which is Rudra is Īśāna; he who is Īśāna—
That Blessed One is Maheśvara. Now, why is he called Oṃkāra? Because as soon as he is uttered, he causes the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) to ascend upward; therefore he is called Oṃkāra.

Now, why is he called Praṇava? Because as soon as he is uttered, he causes the Brahman consisting of the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharvāṅgiras [Vedas] to bow down and incline toward the Brāhmaṇas; therefore he is called Praṇava.

Now, why is it called "all-pervading" (*sarvavyāpin*)? Because as soon as it is uttered, it permeates and penetrates everything—just as oil pervades a ball of ground meal—and being interwoven with all that has a tranquil form, it is therefore called "all-pervading. Now, why is it called "infinite" (*ananta*)? Because as soon as it is uttered, its end is not perceived horizontally, upwards, or downwards; therefore it is called "infinite."

Now, why is it called *tāra*? Because as soon as it is uttered, it delivers (*tārayati*) and protects (*trāyate*) one from the great fears of saṃsāra—namely, conception, birth, disease, old age, and death; therefore it is called *tāra*. Now, why is it called *śukla*? Because as soon as it is uttered, it purifies (*klādate*) and causes purification (*klāmayati*); therefore it is called *śukla*. Now, why is it called *sūkṣma*? Because as soon as it is uttered, having become subtle (*sūkṣma*), it presides over all bodies and touches all limbs; therefore it is called *sūkṣma*.

Now, why is it called *vaidyuta*? Because even as it is being uttered, it illuminates (*dyotayati*) the manifest great darkness; therefore it is called *vaidyuta*. Now, why is it called *paraṃ brahma*? Because it is supreme (*param*), beyond the lower (*aparam*), and the ultimate refuge (*parāyaṇam*); because it is vast (*bṛhat*) and causes [all things] to grow by means of its vastness (*bṛhatyā*); therefore it is called *paraṃ brahma*. Now, why is it called *ekaḥ* (the One)? Because, having consumed all vital breaths (*prāṇān*), through that act of consuming, it—as the unborn (*ajaḥ*)—both emits and withdraws them.
Some go to sacred fords; some go southward, westward, northward, or eastward. Of all these, their meeting place is here.
He alone exists as one and moves among living beings; therefore he is called "One."
Now, why is he called Rudra? Because his form is swiftly perceived by the seers and by no others who are devoted to him, therefore he is called Rudra.
Now, why is he called Īśāna? Because he rules over all the gods by means of his sovereign and generative powers (śaktis). "Without striking, the hero is praised; like cows that have been milked."
"He is the ruler of this moving world, the ruler of that which stands still, O Indra"—therefore he is called Īśāna.

Now, why is he called Bhagavān Maheśvara? Because through his grace he honors and favors his devotees with knowledge; because he creates and emits speech; and because, having renounced all objective states, he dwells in the Great through self-knowledge and the sovereignty of yoga.
Therefore he is magnified; thus he is called the Blessed Lord Maheśvara. This is the conduct of Rudra.
The one God who extends across all directions was indeed born first; he is within the womb. He alone has been born, he is yet to be born; facing every direction, he stands with faces on all sides.

There is one Rudra, not a second; he who rules these worlds by his sovereign powers stands facing all beings. Having created all worlds, the Protector withdraws them at the time of the end. He alone presides over every womb, by whom all this universe moves about.
Having perceived that Lord, the boon-granting God worthy of praise, one attains this ultimate peace.
Having abandoned patience—the root of the web of causes—and having established through the intellect that which was accumulated, they call Rudra the oneness with Rudra;
he who is eternal and ancient, who by means of nourishment and vigor causes the cattle to be released from the snares of death.

Thus, by means of this self and this three-and-a-half measure, one effects peace and the liberation from the bonds of the individual soul (*paśu-pāśa-vimokṣaṇa*). That which is the first measure, having Brahman as its deity and red in color—he who meditates upon it constantly shall go to the station of Brahman. That which is the second measure, having Viṣṇu as its deity and black in color—he who meditates upon it constantly shall go to the station of Viṣṇu.
That third measure, which has Īśāna as its deity and is tawny in color—he who meditates on it constantly shall go to the station of Īśāna.

That fourth-and-a-half measure, which has all the deities as its object, which has become unmanifest, which moves through the ether, and which is pure and resembles crystal in color—he who meditates on it constantly shall go to the station that is free from disease. Sages speak of this as the object of worship; they say there is no grasping of it. This is the path ordained by the higher way, by which the gods go, by which the ancestors go, by which the seers go—to the supreme, the lower, and the ultimate refuge.
And thus:
"In the center of the heart, the size of the tip of a hair, is the universal god, golden-hued and most excellent.
Those wise ones who behold Him abiding within themselves—for them alone there is peace, and not for others. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.13–14)

Having abandoned both anger and craving, as well as patience and impatience—the root of the web of causes—and having established through the intellect that which has been accumulated in Rudra, they call that state of oneness "Rudra. For Rudra is indeed the eternal, ancient restrainer by means of vigor, strength, and austerity; he is fire, and he is ash, and he is the wind.

Ash is water; ash is the earth; ash is the sky; indeed, all this is ash. Ash is the mind and these are the senses. Because one should touch one's limbs with ash as this Pāśupata vow, therefore it is Brahman. This is that Pāśupata [vow] for the sake of liberation from the bonds of the individual soul (paśu).
Rudra who is in the fire, who is within the waters, who has entered the herbs and the plants—
he who fashioned all these worlds, to that Rudra, to Agni, let there be homage!
Rudra who is in the fire, Rudra who is within the waters, Rudra who has entered the herbs and the plants.
To that Rudra who fashioned all these worlds, to that Rudra, salutation after salutation! To the Rudra who is in the waters, the Rudra who is in the plants, the Rudra who is in the trees;

by whom, O Rudra, the world was held aloft, and by whom the earth—held as two-fold and three-fold—is supported, along with the serpents in the intermediate space: to that Rudra indeed, salutation after salutation!
Having thoroughly served his head and that which is the heart, Atharvan impels [the breath] upward from the brain;
it is the supreme honor from the top of the head.
That indeed is the head of Atharvan, the divine casket, cast forth.
The vital breath protects that [Self] as far as the head, and likewise the mind;

neither by the divine host protected in heaven, nor by the intermediate spaces, nor by these earths is it guarded. In Him this entire universe is woven like warp and woof; there is nothing else whatsoever beyond Him.
There is nothing prior to Him, nor anything beyond Him; there was nothing that existed, nor will there be anything that shall come to be, other than He who is.
With a thousand feet and a single head, he alone pervades and repeatedly encompasses this entire world.
From the Imperishable (akṣara) time is born; from time, the Pervasive One is said to arise.
For the Blessed Lord Rudra is indeed the Pervasive One; when Rudra lies down, assuming the state of enjoyment, then all creatures are withdrawn.

Upon exhalation there is darkness; from darkness, water; when water is churned with a finger, from that churning comes cold; from cold being churned, foam arises; from foam, the cosmic egg arises; from the egg, Brahmā arises; from Brahmā, Vāyu; from Vāyu, the syllable Oṃ;
from Oṃ, the Sāvitrī; from the Sāvitrī, the Gāyatrī; and from the Gāyatrī, the worlds arise.
They honor austerity and truth, and they distill the honey that is eternal;
for this indeed is the supreme austerity:
*āpo jyotī raso 'mṛtaṃ brahma bhūr bhuvaḥ svar oṃ namaḥ*. SirUp_44

The Brahmin who studies this Atharvaśiras becomes learned in the Vedas even if he was previously unlearned; he becomes initiated even if he was previously uninitiated. He becomes purified by fire, he becomes purified by wind, he becomes purified by the sun, he becomes purified by Soma, he becomes purified by truth, he becomes known by all the gods, and he is meditated upon by all the Vedas.

He becomes one who has bathed in all sacred fords; by him all sacrifices have been performed; sixty thousand recitations of the Gāyatrī have been completed; hundreds of thousands of recitations of the Rudras from the Itihāsas and Purāṇas have been completed;
and ten thousand recitations of the Praṇavas have been completed.
He purifies the lineage of his vision;
he purifies it up to the seventh generation of ancestors—so says the Blessed One. Having recited the Atharvaśiras even once, one becomes pure, purified, and fit for sacred rites.
By reciting it a second time, one attains leadership over the Gaṇas.
Having recited this a third time, one enters in this very manner: "Oṃ Truth! Oṃ Truth! Oṃ Truth!
Thus ends the Śiras Upaniṣad in the Atharvaveda. SirUp_45
